18 An engine transforms thermal energy into mechanical work. The engine takes in thermal energy
Qin from a heat source and gives out thermal energy Qout to a heat sink, producing useful work W.

hints: Look at the arrows in the diagram: $Q_{in}$ flows into the engine from the heat source, while $W$ and $Q_{out}$ flow out of the engine.
Recall that efficiency is $\text{useful output} / \text{total energy input}$ and decide which symbol is the useful mechanical output and which symbol is the total thermal energy supplied.
Check whether the wasted heat $Q_{out}$ should be added to, subtracted from, or excluded from the energy supplied when forming the denominator.
walkthrough: Identify the energy flows: total energy supplied to the engine is $Q_{in}$, useful energy obtained is mechanical work $W$, and wasted energy rejected is $Q_{out}$.
State the governing rule: $\text{efficiency} = \dfrac{\text{useful output energy}}{\text{total input energy}}$.
Substitute this engine's quantities: useful output $= W$ and total input $= Q_{in}$, so $\text{efficiency} = \dfrac{W}{Q_{in}}$.
Note that $Q_{out}$ is not part of the input, so it does not belong in the denominator; energy conservation gives $Q_{in} = W + Q_{out}$.

A.explanation: Adding $Q_{in} + Q_{out}$ treats wasted heat as extra input, but the only energy supplied to the engine is $Q_{in}$.

B.explanation: Using $Q_{in} - Q_{out}$ as input is wrong because $Q_{in} - Q_{out}$ equals $W$ by energy conservation, which would always give efficiency 1.

C.explanation: Efficiency is useful output divided by total input, so $W$ divided by $Q_{in}$.

D.explanation: Using $Q_{out}$ as denominator treats the waste heat rejected to the sink as the energy input.
